questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why a wood panel is coated before painting
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a wood panel is sealed before painting begins
questions.stem: A workshop specification for an oak cabinet door calls for a sealed and level ground before any colour is laid on.

options.text: The sealing coat limits moisture exchange so the wood cannot swell or shrink and crack the paint film.
The sealer leaves a slick surface so the brush glides and the paint is less likely to be pulled off.
options.misconception: believes a slick surface is what protects the paint film

options.text: The coat hides the grain so the finished door reads as one smooth sheet of pale stone.
options.misconception: thinks the ground is a decorative imitation of stone

options.text: The white layer warms the underpainting so the finished colour avoids the coldness of bare wood.
options.misconception: assumes the ground warms the colour rather than sealing it

questions.explanation: Wood swells and shrinks with humidity, so an unsealed panel would lift its paint film. Sealing and sizing stabilise the surface. Slickness, stone imitation and warm tinting are not the purpose of a ground.
questions.hint: Think about what the wood does across a wet winter.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a ground gives the painter to work on
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the volume of ground required for a measured panel
questions.stem: A 2.0 square metre panel is to receive two coats of ground, and each coat consumes 0.4 litres per square metre. How many litres are needed?
questions.explanation: One coat over 2.0 square metres at 0.4 litres per square metre consumes 0.8 litres. Two coats therefore need 1.6 litres, allowing nothing for wastage or spillage.
questions.hint: Work out one coat first, then double it.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What an underdrawing is for
questions.learningObjective: Identify the purpose the underdrawing serves in a panel painting

stimulus.body: Infrared reflectography over the panel shows a fine network of lines that matches the final figures but adds a grid of small marks across the background. The paint layer sits directly on top of this network.

questions.stem: Given the conservation report, what is the underdrawing on this panel for?

options.text: To block in the composition and fix the proportions before colour is committed.
To record the final colours in outline so they need no further correction.
options.misconception: confuses the underdrawing with a colour record

options.text: To sign the panel and date the work for the workshop's ledger.
options.misconception: treats the underdrawing as a signature or a date

options.text: To test the absorbency of the ground before the first colour is applied.
options.misconception: believes the underdrawing measures the ground's absorbency

questions.explanation: An underdrawing sets out the composition so the painter can correct the layout before committing colour. It does not record finished colours, carry a signature, or test the ground.
questions.hint: Look at what the lines do, not at what they record.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a sinopia records
questions.learningObjective: Describe what a sinopia underlayer preserves for later study
questions.stem: A conservator is asked to explain, in writing, what the dark underlayer on a panel preserves for later study.

answer.exemplar: A sinopia is the reddish-brown earth pigment painted directly on the ground, recording the composition in brush and line before any colour. It preserves the working design, the artist's corrections, and the first decisions about placing, so a scholar can study how the picture was built up rather than only how it finished.

questions.explanation: A good answer defines the sinopia, links it to the working design, and explains why that record is useful to study. It should not claim the sinopia is the finished picture.
questions.hint: Say what layer it is and what it preserves.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why a fresco wall is painted in daily sections
questions.learningObjective: Read a section log and infer the rule behind daily fresco work
questions.stem: A plasterer's log records 1.2 metre wide sections completed one after another across 6 days, with the colour layer added to each section the same day it was laid.

options.text: Each section must be painted while its plaster is still fresh so the colour bonds into the wall.
Each section is given a day so the paint can dry fully before the next is begun.
options.misconception: reads a daily rate as a drying schedule

options.text: Each section is charged separately so the client can pay by the day.
options.misconception: assumes the daily sections are for payment

options.text: Each section is a separate panel that is later moved into the wall.
options.misconception: believes each section is a portable panel

questions.explanation: Fresh plaster takes the colour into its own surface, so painting must follow the plastering the same day. A drying schedule, a payment method and a movable panel all contradict the single-day sequence.
questions.hint: Consider what happens if the paint is added the next day.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why painting on dry plaster is less durable
questions.learningObjective: Choose the mechanism by which paint on dry plaster fails
questions.stem: A restorer finds a wall painted over plaster that had already cured for a month. The colour sits as a thin skin that peels away in sheets. Which account best explains the failure?

options.text: The colour never entered the plaster, so it bonded only to a dusty surface layer and later let go.
The plaster expanded as it dried and pushed the colour away from the wall.
options.misconception: claims the wall pushed the paint off through expansion

options.text: The colour was mixed with a medium that dissolved the plaster beneath it.
options.misconception: blames the paint medium for dissolving the plaster

options.text: The wall was painted in a room that was too warm, so the colour blistered and lifted.
options.misconception: attributes the lifting to room temperature alone

questions.explanation: Paint applied to cured plaster has no wet surface to sink into, so it sits on the surface and adheres only weakly. Expansion, dissolving and heat blistering describe different faults that the peeling sheets do not match.
questions.hint: Ask whether the colour is inside the plaster or on it.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why a tempera panel was finished in oil
questions.learningObjective: Explain what the oil finish achieved over a tempera panel
questions.stem: A panel painted in egg tempera in the 1500s was later given a layer of drying oil. What did that oil layer achieve?

options.text: It added depth and sheen and slowed the drying of colours that had been laid too thick.
It replaced the tempera film so that the panel could be repainted in oils.
options.misconception: assumes the oil film replaces the tempera beneath it

options.text: It waterproofed the wood so the panel could be stored in a damp room.
options.misconception: treats the oil layer as a water barrier for the wood

options.text: It removed the tempera's dryness so the panel would not crack when hung.
options.misconception: believes the oil layer prevents cracking of the panel

questions.explanation: Oil glazes over tempera deepen the colour and add sheen, protecting a dry matte film. Replacing the painting, sealing the wood and preventing cracks are not what the added oil achieves.
questions.hint: Think about the difference between tempera and oil in depth.

questions.topic: Why a wood panel is coated before painting
questions.learningObjective: Compute the sealer needed for a panel of stated size
questions.stem: A joiner measures a 1.2 metre wide oak panel and plans a sealing coat that covers 0.5 litres per square metre. The panel is 0.9 metre high, so how many litres of sealer are needed?
questions.explanation: The panel covers 1.2 by 0.9 square metres, which is 1.08 square metres. At 0.5 litres per square metre the sealer needed is 0.54 litres.
questions.hint: Find the area of the panel before the rate.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a ground gives the painter to work on
questions.learningObjective: Infer the working property of a ground from a workshop note

stimulus.body: A workshop note records that a new panel was sized after gesso, that a thin layer of gesso was brushed on and levelled, and that two further coats followed. The final surface took an egg tempera brushstroke without the colour sliding.

questions.stem: According to the workshop note, what does the ground give the painter to work on?

options.text: A firm, even, slightly toothed surface that grips the brush and keeps the colour where it is placed.
A completely smooth and slick surface so that brush hairs do not catch and drag.
options.misconception: believes the ideal ground is slick and unbroken

options.text: A soft and spongy surface that soaks the colour in deeply and quickly.
options.misconception: thinks the ground should swallow the colour quickly

options.text: A warm tinted surface that colours the first coat as the brush passes over it.
options.misconception: assumes the ground should tint the paint colour

questions.explanation: The note stresses that the colour did not slide, which means the ground grips and holds it. A slick, spongy or tinted ground would produce sliding, soaking or a colour shift, none of which the note reports.
questions.hint: The note tells you what happened to the brushstroke.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What an underdrawing is for
questions.learningObjective: Explain what an underdrawing contributes to a panel painting
questions.stem: A studio manager asks for a written account of what an underdrawing contributes to a panel painting.

answer.exemplar: An underdrawing is the first working image laid on the prepared ground, usually in a dark earth pigment or in metalpoint. It fixes the composition, the placing of the figures and the proportions while these can still be changed cheaply, giving the painter a plan to revise and the later viewer a record of the working process.

questions.explanation: A good answer identifies the underdrawing as a working plan for composition and proportion, and notes its value for later study. It should not present the underdrawing as the finished picture or as a layer of colour.
questions.hint: Describe what it is and what the painter can still change.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a sinopia records
questions.learningObjective: Interpret construction marks in a sinopia as evidence of transfer
questions.stem: A laboratory compares two panels. On one, the dark underlayer shows a single freehand figure; on the other it shows a squared grid, a compass circle and then the figure drawn freehand over the grid. What does the second panel's underlayer record?

options.text: A careful transfer of a prepared design, showing the artist worked from a planned construction.
A trial attempt at the final colour scheme, abandoned before the picture was painted.
options.misconception: reads the dark layer as an abandoned colour sketch

options.text: A set of workshop instructions for the apprentice who later painted the panel.
options.misconception: treats the underlayer as written instructions for assistants

options.text: An artist's signature and the date the panel was completed.
options.misconception: mistakes the compass circle for a signature and date

questions.explanation: The grid and compass are construction aids, so the second panel shows a transferred plan rather than invention. An abandoned colour sketch, a set of instructions and a signature would not leave a squared construction.
questions.hint: Ask what a grid and a compass are used for.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why a fresco wall is painted in daily sections
questions.learningObjective: Select a workable plan for laying and painting fresco sections
questions.stem: A fresco team must paint 7 sections of plaster on 7 consecutive days. Each morning they lay the plaster, and they must add the colour before the section is dry. Which plan works?

options.text: Lay and paint one section each morning, finishing the week's work on the seventh day.
Lay all seven sections on the first morning and paint them one per day afterwards.
options.misconception: plans to plaster everything before any painting starts

options.text: Lay one section each morning but paint only every third section to keep a steady hand.
options.misconception: believes fresh sections can be left waiting for days

options.text: Lay the plaster in the afternoon and paint each section the following morning.
options.misconception: believes next-morning painting is still painting wet plaster

questions.explanation: Colour must meet plaster that is still workable, so laying and painting belong to the same day. Plastering everything first, skipping sections, or waiting until the next morning all leave the surface too firm to take the colour.
questions.hint: The wet section and the brush have to meet on the same day.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why painting on dry plaster is less durable
questions.learningObjective: Explain why colour lifts from a cured plaster wall
questions.stem: A restorer is asked why a colour layer applied to a wall a month after plastering keeps flaking away in large pieces.

options.text: The cured plaster no longer takes the colour into its pores, so adhesion is weak.
The cured plaster keeps drawing moisture from the colour, which makes it crack.
options.misconception: blames the cured plaster for sucking moisture out of the paint

options.text: The colour on a dry wall is exposed to dust that settles into it and lifts it.
options.misconception: claims settled dust is what lifts the paint

options.text: The dry wall is colder, so the colour contracts faster than when it was applied.
options.misconception: suggests cold walls make the paint contract

questions.explanation: Adhesion depends on the colour sinking into a surface that is still open. Once the plaster has cured there is no open surface, so the film sits weakly and peels. Moisture draw, dust and cold are not the mechanism here.
questions.hint: Consider the moment the plaster was no longer fresh.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why a tempera panel was finished in oil
questions.learningObjective: Compute the depth of an oil finish applied in several glazes
questions.stem: A 0.5 metre wide panel is finished with a sequence of oil glazes, each adding 0.02 mm of film, and 5 glazes are applied. What total film depth in millimetres results?
questions.explanation: Each glaze adds 0.02 mm, so five glazes add 0.1 mm in total. This is the depth of the added oil film, not the depth of the tempera beneath it.
questions.hint: Multiply the number of glazes by the film each adds.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why a wood panel is coated before painting
questions.learningObjective: Use a condition report to justify sealing a damaged panel

stimulus.body: The report notes that the panel's ground is sound but the wood beneath the lower rail shows a fine line of cleavage along the grain. The area has not been painted for some time.

questions.stem: According to the condition report, why must the panel be coated before the rail is repainted?

options.text: The bare wood takes up moisture unevenly and can move, so a sealed ground keeps new paint attached.
The exposed grain absorbs oil so quickly that the new colour would dry before it can be spread.
options.misconception: believes the bare wood starves the paint of oil

options.text: The uncoated wood shows the old nail holes clearly enough to spoil the finished surface.
options.misconception: claims the coating is needed to hide old fixings

options.text: The wood has grown sooty and a coat of ground is the only way to lighten it.
options.misconception: assumes the ground is used to bleach sooty wood

questions.explanation: Bare wood that has lost its ground responds to moisture and moves with the grain, which threatens a fresh paint film. Absorbing oil, hiding fixings and bleaching soot do not explain the cleavage reported.
questions.hint: The report mentions movement along the grain.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a ground gives the painter to work on
questions.learningObjective: Describe how a prepared ground affects the behaviour of a brush
questions.stem: A printmaker asks in writing what a prepared ground contributes to the way a brush behaves on a panel.

answer.exemplar: A prepared ground gives the brush a firm, even and slightly textured surface, so the bristles meet something consistent across the whole panel. Paint sits in the tooth of the ground rather than sliding, which lets the painter keep an edge, judge the load of the brush and build a passage evenly instead of watching the colour slump or run.

questions.explanation: A good answer ties the ground to brush control, describing an even, gripping surface and what that does for edges and even passages. It should not describe the ground as a colour or as a support for drawing only.
questions.hint: Focus on how the brush behaves on it.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What an underdrawing is for
questions.learningObjective: Interpret the spread of underdrawn lines across a panel
questions.stem: A comparison of two infrared images shows that on the first the lines under the paint run only where the figures are; on the second they also cross the sky and the floor, and the figures sit exactly on them.

options.text: The second panel's design was laid over a full underlying structure rather than drawn freehand.
The second panel's underdrawing was added later as a correction of a finished picture.
options.misconception: reads extra lines as later correction of a finished work

options.text: The second panel's artist simply drew more lines than the first artist did.
options.misconception: explains extra lines as a habit of the draughtsman

options.text: The second panel's paint has faded, leaving its own brushwork visible in the infrared.
options.misconception: mistakes faded brushwork for underdrawing

questions.explanation: Lines crossing the whole picture with the figures aligned to them suggest a transferred grid used to lay out the design. A later correction, a drawing habit and faded brushwork would not produce that alignment.
questions.hint: Ask what the extra lines are doing under the figures.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a sinopia records
questions.learningObjective: Read revisions in a sinopia as a record of staged design
questions.stem: A scholar asks how a conservator should read a sinopia that shows an abandoned first figure and a second figure drawn over the corrections.

options.text: As a record of a design developed in stages, where the first idea was changed before colour was applied.
As evidence that the picture was repainted by a different hand for the market.
options.misconception: reads revisions as a later seller's repaint

options.text: As proof that the panel was reused from an older, unrelated composition.
options.misconception: assumes the panel was recycled from another design

options.text: As a record of the colours the painter finally rejected and never used.
options.misconception: takes the sinopia for a record of abandoned colour

questions.explanation: Corrections and overdrawings show the design being worked out on the panel itself, which is exactly what a sinopia preserves. A repaint, a reused panel and a list of rejected colours would not be recorded in a single drawing layer.
questions.hint: A sinopia preserves decisions, not the finished picture.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why a fresco wall is painted in daily sections
questions.learningObjective: Explain why fresco colour must follow plastering on the same day
questions.stem: A mason asks why the team on a chapel wall paints only the section of plaster laid that same morning.

options.text: Because colour must be set into plaster that is still soft enough to take it.
Because painters need a rest between laying and painting for the shoulder's sake.
options.misconception: explains the daily section as rest for the painter

options.text: Because the old paint beneath must be sanded back before the new one is applied.
options.misconception: believes the daily cycle is about sanding old paint

options.text: Because the light in the chapel only reaches the wall in the morning hours.
options.misconception: claims the daily section is a lighting constraint

questions.explanation: Colour bonds when it is worked into a surface that is still open, so painting follows plastering on the same day. Rest, sanding and the direction of daylight are not the working reason for the daily section.
questions.hint: Think about when the surface is still receptive.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why painting on dry plaster is less durable
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the proportion of a wall affected by flaking
questions.stem: A survey finds that flaking covers 1.5 square metres of a 20 square metre wall. What percentage of the wall area is affected?
questions.explanation: The affected area of 1.5 square metres divided by the total 20 square metres gives 0.075, which is 7.5 per cent. Using the wall's total area as the denominator is what makes this meaningful.
questions.hint: Divide the flaking area by the whole wall area.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why a tempera panel was finished in oil
questions.learningObjective: Identify the effect of an added oil layer on a tempera surface

stimulus.body: The record notes that the panel was completed in egg tempera, that the surface was left matte, and that a thin layer of drying oil was later applied and polished. Under raking light the coloured passages appear noticeably deeper than in the 1900s record photograph.

questions.stem: According to the treatment record, what did the added oil achieve on this tempera panel?

options.text: It deepened the colour and added sheen over a matte tempera surface.
It removed the tempera film and left only the oil paint underneath.
options.misconception: thinks the oil layer stripped away the tempera

options.text: It kept the panel airtight so it could be stored in a damp room.
options.misconception: treats the oil film as a damp-proof seal

options.text: It stiffened the tempera so the panel would not flex in the frame.
options.misconception: believes the oil coat stiffened the wood panel

questions.explanation: The record contrasts matte tempera with deeper colour and sheen after the oil, which is what a glaze does. Stripping the film, sealing against damp and stiffening the panel are not what a glaze does.
questions.hint: Compare the surface before and after the oil.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why a wood panel is coated before painting
questions.learningObjective: Explain the long-term effect of sealing a new board
questions.stem: A panel maker asks in writing why the first layer on a new board matters so much to the life of the picture.

answer.exemplar: The first sealing and sizing layers close the raw wood so that moisture cannot move in and out of the board under the paint. With the movement damped, the ground and the films above it stay in one piece instead of cracking and lifting, which is why a board that was skipped or badly sized will fail long before the colour itself wears away.

questions.explanation: A good answer links the coating to moisture control and to the long-term stability of the films above it, and notes what fails without it. It should not describe the coating as a decorative finish or as a colour.
questions.hint: Say what the board does that the coating stops.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a ground gives the painter to work on
questions.learningObjective: Infer what a ground must grip from a comparison of two panels
questions.stem: Two test panels are prepared. On the first the ground is smooth and polished to a shine; on the second it is left matt and slightly textured. The tempera on the first slid and feathered, while the second held clean edges.

options.text: The painter needs a textured, gripping surface so the colour stays where it is placed.
The painter needs a highly polished surface so that brush hairs never catch.
options.misconception: believes the ideal ground is polished to a shine

options.text: The painter needs a thicker ground so that more colour can be absorbed.
options.misconception: thinks a thicker ground grips the brush better

options.text: The painter needs a darker ground so that the pale tempera shows clearly.
options.misconception: believes a dark ground is what keeps edges clean

questions.explanation: Sliding and feathering on the polished panel and clean edges on the matt one show that grip comes from texture, not from gloss, thickness or colour. The comparison isolates the surface finish as the deciding factor.
questions.hint: Compare what happened to the colour on each panel.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What an underdrawing is for
questions.learningObjective: Decide whether pinholes show a transferred or a free underdrawing
questions.stem: A conservator wants to know whether the underdrawing of a panel was a free invention or a transfer, given that faint pinholes run in straight rows across the ground and the figure aligns with them.

options.text: It was a transfer, because the pinholes mark a pricked pattern the artist traced.
It was a free invention, because pinholes in the ground are always accidental damage.
options.misconception: dismisses regular pinholes as random damage

options.text: It was a free invention, because a transferred design would have shown a continuous line.
options.misconception: believes transfer always leaves unbroken outlines

options.text: It was a transfer, because the presence of a figure proves the pattern was used.
options.misconception: treats the figure as proof of transfer

questions.explanation: Rows of pinholes are the standard way of transferring a design, and the figure sitting on them confirms the pattern was used. Random damage, a missing outline and the mere presence of a figure prove nothing about transfer.
questions.hint: Pin holes in rows come from a specific transfer method.

questions.topic: What a sinopia records
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a sinopia reveals about the making of a panel
questions.stem: A visitor asks what the reddish-brown layer beneath a finished panel picture tells us about its making.

options.text: It records the composition the painter first worked out before applying colour.
It shows which pigments were available in the shop on the day of painting.
options.misconception: treats the sinopia as a record of available pigments

options.text: It proves the panel was once covered by a cloth and re-lined.
options.misconception: reads the underlayer as evidence of re-lining

options.text: It fixes the date the panel was finished, since the earth used is dated.
options.misconception: claims the sinopia dates the panel precisely

questions.explanation: The sinopia is a working drawing in earth pigment, so it preserves the design as first planned. Pigment stocks, re-lining and a date derived from earth are all things a ground layer cannot tell us.
questions.hint: The layer records a drawing, not a document.

questions.topic: Why painting on dry plaster is less durable
questions.learningObjective: Explain a difference in flaking using a site note

stimulus.body: A site note records that a section of wall was plastered in the morning of one day, that the first colour was added the following morning, and that this section now lifts in flakes while the sections painted the same day are sound.

questions.stem: According to the site note, what explains the difference between the flaking section and the sound ones?

options.text: The colour on the flaking section sat on a hardened surface instead of entering fresh plaster.
The colour on the flaking section was made with too much oil and could not dry.
options.misconception: blames excess oil for the flaking

options.text: The colour on the flaking section was applied in a colder part of the week.
options.misconception: attributes the failure to cold weather alone

options.text: The colour on the flaking section was thinner than on the other sections.
options.misconception: assumes thinner colour causes the flaking

questions.explanation: The one-day-later section is the only one painted on cured plaster, so it is the only one where the colour could not enter the surface. Oil, cold and thin colour are not mentioned in the note.
questions.hint: Only one section was painted the day after plastering.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why a tempera panel was finished in oil
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a tempera panel was finished with oil
questions.stem: A conservator is asked in writing why a tempera panel in a damp church needed an oil finish to survive.

answer.exemplar: Egg tempera dries to a thin, matte and somewhat brittle film that is vulnerable to handling and to damp, and it cannot be re-worked once set. A thin oil layer over it adds depth to the colour, gives a tougher and slightly more flexible surface, and allows the picture to be varnished and cleaned, protecting the tempera underneath.

questions.explanation: A good answer explains that the oil layer protects and enriches a dry, matte tempera film, and links that to handling and damp. It should not suggest the oil replaced the tempera or made the panel waterproof.
questions.hint: Compare the surfaces before and after the oil.

The unsealed panel was painted with a coarser brush that left a drier, less flexible film.

options.misconception: suggests storage orientation explains the cracking

options.text: The unsealed panel was cleaned more often, and cleaning thickens and cracks paint.
options.misconception: claims frequent cleaning causes the cracking

questions.explanation: Only the unsealed panel was free to respond to damp, so only it carried the paint film into the cracking pattern seen. Brush coarseness, storage orientation and cleaning do not explain a difference in movement.

options.misconception: blames the drawing material rather than the surface

options.text: Check whether the panel has been oiled, since oil makes the surface slippery.
options.misconception: recommends oiling a surface that already slips

questions.explanation: A ground that is too smooth or too weak lets the stroke slide, so surface preparation is the first thing to check. Warmth, charcoal grading and oiling a slipping surface are not the logical first move.

options.misconception: suggests the daily rule is about inspection

questions.topic: Why painting on dry plaster is less durable
questions.learningObjective: Explain why fresco on a dry wall outlasts paint on a dry wall
questions.stem: A building owner asks in writing why fresco on a dry wall outlasts paint on a dry wall in the same building.

answer.exemplar: A fresco colour is worked into plaster that is still open, so it becomes part of the wall's own body rather than a film sitting on it. The same colour on a cured wall can only rest on the surface, where it is exposed to wear, to handling and to the small movements of the building, and it therefore peels away in sheets.

questions.explanation: A good answer contrasts colour that has entered the plaster with colour resting on a cured surface, and links that to the way each fails. It should not rest on claims about a special binding medium.
questions.hint: Compare where the colour sits in each case.

options.text: The first panel carries an added oil or resin layer that has filled the minute texture of the surface.
The first panel was painted with a medium that naturally takes a high gloss.
options.misconception: explains the shine as the tempera medium's own gloss

options.text: The first panel is simply cleaner, and dust on the second dulls it.
options.misconception: attributes the flatness to dust on the second panel

options.text: The first panel was repainted, and the upper film is a later addition.
options.misconception: reads the film as a full repainting rather than a varnish

questions.explanation: A film that fills fine texture and catches raking light is a layer laid over the picture, which is what a varnish is. Medium gloss, dust and repainting would each leave a different surface.
questions.hint: Look at what the light does in the small hollows.

options.text: Test the panel for movement, then remove the failing films, then size and reground.
Strip first, then test for movement, then ground without sizing.
options.misconception: grounds without sizing after stripping

options.text: Ground first to fill the cracks, then test, then strip the new ground away.
options.misconception: grounds before diagnosing the cause

options.text: Test and ground first, then strip everything including the sound paint.
options.misconception: strips sound paint along with the failing film

questions.explanation: The cause must be identified before stripping, and the ground system is replaced in order, with sizing between wood and ground. Grounding early or stripping sound paint discards evidence and good material.
questions.hint: Diagnose first, then treat the panel in the proper order.

options.misconception: claims doubling the ground prevents warping

questions.learningObjective: Explain why fresco work is organised in daily sections
questions.stem: A project manager asks in writing why the plastering team cannot simply cover a whole wall in one push.

answer.exemplar: Plaster laid in one long run would be too large a body of wet work to finish and paint within a single day, and the surface would set before the colour could be worked into it. Working in giornate, one day's section at a time, lets each area be laid, levelled and painted while it is still workable, so the wall advances in a sequence that matches the material.

questions.explanation: A good answer connects the daily section to the practical limit of a day's plastering and to the need to paint while the surface is open. It should not present the daily section as a matter of payment or of lighting.

options.text: The colour is resting on a cured surface, so the plaster beneath is not holding it.
The colour has burned, leaving pale brittle patches where the heat was strongest.
options.misconception: explains the patches as heat damage

options.text: The plaster has dissolved under the colour, leaving hollows that later broke away.
options.misconception: claims the plaster dissolved beneath the paint

options.text: The colour is being lifted by salt crystals forming inside the wall.
options.misconception: attributes the lifting to salt efflorescence

questions.explanation: Circular losses spreading from cracks, over hard pale plaster, are the signature of a film sitting on a cured surface and letting go at weak points. Burning, dissolving plaster and salt crystals each leave different evidence.

options.text: Clean gently with a suitable solvent and renew the protective oil or varnish layer.
Wash the panel with warm water and detergent, then repaint the worn areas.
options.misconception: recommends washing and repainting a fragile film

options.text: Scrub the powdery areas with abrasive powder, then apply a thick oil coating.
options.misconception: recommends abrasive scrubbing of a fragile film

options.text: Apply a further heavy coat of oil without cleaning, sealing the powder into the surface.
options.misconception: advances sealing a dirty, powdery surface

questions.explanation: A powdery, matte tempera film needs gentle cleaning and a fresh protective layer, which is what a conservator would do. Washing, scrubbing and sealing dirt in with more oil all risk damaging the remaining film.

questions.topic: What a sinopia records
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a sinopia is more informative than the finished picture
questions.stem: A conservator is asked in writing to explain why the sinopia of a panel is often more informative than the finished picture.

answer.exemplar: The finished picture is the result of many decisions, and the later layers hide the earlier ones, so a viewer sees only the last surviving version of each passage. The sinopia is the first statement of the design, made before colour could be tested, and it therefore preserves the artist's earliest thinking, the corrections made to it, and the parts of the composition that were later covered or abandoned.

questions.explanation: A good answer explains that the sinopia preserves the earliest, unaltered statement of the design, and that later layers hide it. It should not claim the sinopia is more accurate or more beautiful than the finished picture.

questions.stem: A training manual asks in writing how an underdrawing differs from the finished picture, and why it is still worth recording.

answer.exemplar: An underdrawing is made first, in a limited palette and usually in a single pigment, and it fixes the layout of the picture while the artist can still change it cheaply. The finished picture is the accumulated result of many later corrections and glazes. Recording the underdrawing therefore preserves the design as it was first planned, and shows which parts were invented, borrowed or revised on the way to the final image.

questions.explanation: A good answer defines the underdrawing as an early, revisable layout and explains its value for study. It should not blur the underdrawing with the finished picture or treat it as a signature.

questions.hint: The only stated difference is the age of the plaster.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why a tempera panel was finished in oil
questions.learningObjective: Compute the oil finish needed for a panel of stated area
questions.stem: A 0.9 square metre panel receives an oil finish applied at 0.1 litres per square metre. How many litres of oil finish are required?
questions.explanation: The panel covers 0.9 square metres, and at 0.1 litres per square metre the finish needed is 0.09 litres. Any figure in litres must follow from the area and the rate together.
questions.hint: Multiply the panel area by the rate for one coat.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why a wood panel is coated before painting
questions.learningObjective: Interpret a difference between re-grounded and untreated areas

stimulus.body: The note records that the panel's edges had been re-ground and re-sized by an earlier restorer, but the central field had not. The painting over the re-treated edges lies flat, while the painting over the untouched field is lifting in small islands.

questions.stem: According to the restorer's note, what does the difference between the two areas show?

options.text: That where the wood was sealed and re-ground, the paint film has stayed attached to the panel.
That the earlier restorer used a better quality of colour than the original painter.
options.misconception: blames the restorer for using better colour

options.text: That the centre of the panel is thicker than the edges of the panel.
options.misconception: infers a difference in paint thickness from the note

options.text: That the earlier restorer repainted the edges of the panel over the original.
options.misconception: assumes the edges were repainted

questions.explanation: The only stated difference is the sealing and re-grounding of the edges, and that is where the film stayed flat. Better colour, a thicker centre and a repainted edge are not supported by the note.
questions.hint: Compare the two areas against the one stated difference.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a ground gives the painter to work on
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a panel must dry between coats of ground
questions.stem: A visiting student asks in writing why a panel must be allowed to dry between each layer of the ground.

answer.exemplar: Each layer of ground has to set before the next is laid, because a fresh coat applied over a wet one mixes with it, traps air and dries unevenly, leaving a soft and lumpy bed. Allowing each coat to dry and be levelled in turn is what produces the firm, even surface that the underdrawing and the colour layers then depend on for their grip and their crisp edges.

questions.explanation: A good answer explains that drying and levelling between coats is what makes the bed firm and even. It should not claim the drying is for the wood's sake or that thick coats replace several thin ones.
questions.hint: Say what happens if the next coat goes on too soon.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What an underdrawing is for
questions.learningObjective: Read an infrared survey as a layer order
questions.stem: An infrared survey of a panel shows the underdrawing running under the painted drapery, the painted drapery running over a chalky priming, and the priming over a panel with visible tool marks from the plane.

options.text: It confirms that the panel was prepared, then primed, then drawn on, then painted.
It shows that the drapery was painted first and the underdrawing added later on top.
options.misconception: reverses the order of drawing and painting

options.text: It shows that the plane marks were made after the painting was finished.
options.misconception: dates the tool marks after the picture

options.text: It shows that the picture was painted on a panel that was never primed at all.
options.misconception: ignores the chalky priming layer

questions.explanation: The survey gives a stack order, with each layer sitting on the one beneath it, ending at the planed board. Reversing that order, dating the tool marks late and denying the priming all contradict the sequence.
questions.hint: Read the survey from the board upwards.

questions.subject: ART_HISTORY
questions.topic: What a sinopia records
questions.learningObjective: Identify what a sinopia shows that the finished picture cannot
questions.stem: A curator asks what a sinopia contributes that the finished picture of the panel cannot show.

options.text: It preserves the artist's first decisions about the composition, before any colour was tested.
It proves the panel was painted in a workshop that shared a common design.
options.misconception: reads the sinopia as proof of a shared workshop design

options.text: It identifies the pigments the painter used, since the earth is mixed with them.
options.misconception: claims the sinopia identifies the pigments used

options.text: It confirms the panel was exported, since the earth was traded across borders.
options.misconception: claims the earth pigment shows where the panel was made

questions.explanation: The sinopia keeps the first statement of the design, which later colour covers. It cannot prove a shared workshop design, identify pigments or show where a panel was made, so those claims overreach.
questions.hint: It preserves decisions, not provenance or materials.
